tip.title: Spot the hidden comparison
tip.text: Writers often explain a new thing by comparing it to something you already know. That is FIGURATIVE language: a tree is not really a bodyguard, but calling it one tells you its job. When you meet a comparison, ask what two things are being compared and what they have in common. Roots "like stilts" means the roots lift the tree the way stilts lift a house. Information texts use these comparisons too, so watch for them even outside stories.

passage.title: Mangroves: The Coast's Bodyguards
passage.text:
Mangroves are trees that grow where the land meets the sea. Unlike most trees, they can live in salty water, standing on tangled roots that rise above the mud like stilts.

Mangroves protect the coast. When a storm pushes big waves toward the shore, the thick wall of roots slows the water down. Studies in the Philippines found that villages behind healthy mangrove forests had far less damage after typhoons than villages where the mangroves had been cut.

Mangroves are also nurseries. Young fish, crabs, and shrimp hide among the roots, where large hunters cannot reach them. Many of the fish that people catch in open water were born in a mangrove forest.

Sadly, many mangrove areas were cleared in the past to make fishponds and resorts. Today, students and fisherfolk in many towns plant mangrove seedlings along the shore. A seedling planted this year may take ten years to become a strong tree, but a forest of them can guard a village for generations.

words.meaning: twisted together in a messy way
words.example: The wires were tangled behind the TV.

words.meaning: a place where young plants or animals are protected while they grow
words.example: The nursery keeps the baby fish safe.

words.meaning: all the people born around the same time; a span of about 25 to 30 years each
words.example: This house has been in our family for three generations.

items.prompt: "Tangled roots that rise above the mud like stilts." What do the roots and stilts have in common?
choices: Both are made of wood from the city.
Both hold something up above the ground or water.
Both are used by circus performers.
Both are soft and easy to bend.
items.why: Stilts are long poles that lift a person or a house above the ground. The roots lift the mangrove above the mud the same way.

items.prompt: How are mangroves DIFFERENT from most other trees?
choices: They have no roots.
They grow only on mountains.
They can live in salty water.
They lose their leaves every year.
items.why: "Unlike most trees, they can live in salty water." The signal word unlike introduces the difference.

items.prompt: The author calls the roots a "thick wall." Why is this a good comparison?
choices: The roots are painted white like a wall.
The roots block and slow the waves the way a wall blocks what hits it.
The roots are flat and smooth.
People build houses on the roots.
items.why: The next words say the wall of roots "slows the water down." A wall stops or slows whatever pushes against it.

items.prompt: Which sentence from the text BEST supports the idea that mangroves reduce typhoon damage?
choices: Mangroves are trees that grow where the land meets the sea.
Studies in the Philippines found that villages behind healthy mangrove forests had far less damage after typhoons than villages where the mangroves had been cut.
Young fish, crabs, and shrimp hide among the roots.
A seedling planted this year may take ten years to become a strong tree.
items.why: The author cites studies comparing villages with and without mangroves. That is direct proof, not just a description.

items.prompt: After a typhoon, how did villages with healthy mangroves compare to villages where mangroves were cut?
choices: They had far less damage.
They had the same amount of damage.
They had more damage.
They had more fish but more damage.
items.why: Studies found villages behind healthy mangroves "had far less damage after typhoons than villages where the mangroves had been cut."

choices: They are large and strong people.
They guard the coast the way a bodyguard protects a person.
They wear uniforms.
They catch fish.
items.why: It is a comparison: mangroves stand between danger (storms) and the village, like a bodyguard.

items.prompt: Which sentence BEST supports the idea that mangroves matter to people who fish in the open sea?
choices: Mangroves are also nurseries.
Many of the fish that people catch in open water were born in a mangrove forest.
Mangroves protect the coast.
Today, students and fisherfolk in many towns plant mangrove seedlings.
items.why: This line connects open-water fishing directly to mangroves: the fish were born there. The other lines do not mention catching fish.

items.prompt: Which sentence BEST supports the idea that people, not storms, destroyed many mangroves?
choices: When a storm pushes big waves toward the shore, the thick wall of roots slows the water down.
Sadly, many mangrove areas were cleared in the past to make fishponds and resorts.
Unlike most trees, they can live in salty water.
A forest of them can guard a village for generations.
items.why: Clearing land "to make fishponds and resorts" is something people do. The other lines are about storms, salt water, or the future.

items.prompt: How is what people do with mangroves TODAY different from what they did in the past?
choices: In the past they planted them; today they cut them.
In the past they cleared them; today they plant seedlings.
In the past they studied them; today they ignore them.
Nothing has changed.
items.why: "Many mangrove areas were cleared in the past... Today, students and fisherfolk in many towns plant mangrove seedlings."

items.prompt: What is the main idea of the WHOLE passage?
choices: Mangroves are strange trees with roots like stilts.
Mangroves are valuable because they protect coasts and shelter young sea life, so people are replanting them.
Fishponds and resorts are bad.
Seedlings take ten years to grow.
items.why: The paragraphs together explain what mangroves do, why they matter, and why people plant them.
